# Page 5^page=5
Coordinate Systems De˝nition of Coordinate Systems Coordinate systems are de˝ned by a set of basis vectors . De˝nitions A coordinate system is orthogonal if its basis vectors intersect at 90◦ angles , i.e., vi · vj = 0, for i ̸= j. A coordinate system is orthonormal if it is orthogonal and its basis vectors have magnitude 1 , i.e., ▶ vi · vj = 0, for i ̸= j, and ▶ |vi| = √vi · vi = 1. 2 34

# Page 6^page=6
Cartesian and generalised coordinate systems Cartesian coordinate system The Cartesian coordinate system is an example of orthonormal coordinate system. i = (1, 0, 0), j = (0, 1, 0), k = (0, 0, 1) De˝nition Generalised coordinate systems do not necessarily have orthogonal coordinate curves. 3 34

# Page 7^page=7
Transformations in 3D Transformations in 3D Let e1, e2, and e3 be basis vectors. Consider the position vector r = x1e1 + x2e2 + x3e3 = ejxj. Rotating the basis vectors, we obtain new basis vectors e′ i, and x′ i = e ′ i · r = e ′ i · ejxj = Lijxj. Where Lij is the transformation matrix . L is orthogonal i.e. LT L = I = LLT . In particular, LijLkj = δik = LjiLjk. We have shown that ∂x′ i ∂xj = Lij and ∂xi ∂x′ j = Lji. 4 34

# Page 8^page=8
Vectors and Scalars Formal De˝nition of vector A quantity v is a vector if its components transform according to v′ i = Lijvj under a rotation of the coordinate axes. Formal De˝nition of scalar A quantity s is a scalar if it is unchanged by a transformation. That is, if s′ = s. 5 34

Dual Basis

# Page 10^page=10
Dual Bases De˝nition. Two bases e1, e2, e3 and e1, e2 , e3 are dual if they satisfy ei · e k = { 0 if i ̸= k, 1 if i = k. In other words, two bases are dual if each vector of one basis is perpendicular to two vectors of the other basis. 6 34

# Page 11^page=11
Constructing dual bases Constructing dual bases Given a basis e1, e2, e3, we are going to prove that there exists a dual basis e1, e2, e3. This will be a constructive proof , meaning we are going to construct this dual basis. First, e1 must be perpendicular to the vectors e2 and e3. Thus, e 1 = m(e2 × e3). Now, we need e1 · e1 = 1, so that m(e1 · (e2 × e3)) = 1. That is m = 1 e1 · (e2 × e3) =: 1 V . 7 34

# Page 12^page=12
Constructing dual bases - Part 2 Constructing dual bases So far, we have e1 = m(e2 × e3), and m = 1 e1 · (e2 × e3) =: 1 V . Here, |V | denotes the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the basis e1, e2, e3. We conclude that e 1 = e2 × e3 e1 · (e2 × e3) = e2 × e3 V . 8 34

# Page 13^page=13
Constructing dual bases - Part 3 Constructing dual bases Similarly, we ˝nd e2 and e3. The dual basis is given by e 1 = e2 × e3 e1 · (e2 × e3) , e 2 = e3 × e1 e2 · (e3 × e1) , e 3 = e1 × e2 e3 · (e1 × e2) . We obtain the formula e i = ej × ek ei · (ej × ek) = ej × ek V , where (i, j, k) is a cyclic permutation of (1, 2, 3). 9 34

# Page 14^page=14
Starting from the dual basis Starting from the dual basis In the same way, we can show e1 = e2 × e3 e1 · (e2 × e3) , e2 = e3 × e1 e2 · (e3 × e1) , e3 = e1 × e2 e3 · (e1 × e2) . Thus, we get the formula ei = ej × ek ei · (ej × ek) = ej × ek V ′ , where (i, j, k) is a cyclic permutation of (1, 2, 3), and |V ′| denotes the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the basis e1, e2, e3. 10 34

# Page 15^page=15
Example Example. Given the basis e1 = 2i1 + i3, e2 = i1 + 3i2, e3 = 4i3, where i1, i2, i3 is an orthonormal basis, ˝nd the dual basis e1, e2, e3. Solution We have e1 = 2i1 + i3, e2 = i1 + 3i2, e3 = 4i3. For simplicity, we write e1 =   2 0 1   , e2 =   1 3 0   , e3 =   0 0 4   . 11 34

# Page 16^page=16
Example - Solution part 2 Solution  Part 2 Recall that the dual basis is given by the formula e i = ej × ek ei · (ej × ek) . Thus, we need the cross products e1 × e2, e2 × e3 and e3 × e1. e1 × e2 =   2 0 1   ×   1 3 0   =   −3 1 6   e2 × e3 =   1 3 0   ×   0 0 4   =   12 −4 0   e3 × e1 =   0 0 4   ×   2 0 1   =   0 8 0   . 12 34

# Page 17^page=17
Example - Solution part 3 Solution  Part 3 Again, e i = ej × ek ei · (ej × ek) . We already computed the cross products, so we still need to ˝nd V . We have V = e1 · (e2 × e3) = e2 · (e3 × e1) = e3 · (e1 × e2). Let us pick one and compute. We know e1 = 2i1 + i3 and e2 × e3 = 12i1 − 4i2. Thus V = e1 · (e2 × e3) = ( 2 0 1 ) · ( 12 −4 0 ) = 24. 13 34

# Page 18^page=18
Example - Solution part 4 Solution  Part 4 Now we can construct the dual basis e 1 = e2 × e3 e1 · (e2 × e3) = 1 24   12 −4 0   =   1/2 −1/6 0   , e 2 = e3 × e1 e2 · (e3 × e1) = 1 24   0 8 0   =   0 1/3 0   , e 3 = e1 × e2 e3 · (e1 × e2) = 1 24   −3 1 6   =   −1/8 1/24 1/4   . 14 34

# Page 19^page=19
Practical Question Your turn! Let i1, i2, i3 be the standard orthonormal basis of R3. Consider the following basis e1 = i1 + 2i2 + 4i3, e2 = i2, e3 = i1 + 2i2 + 5i3. Find the dual basis e1, e2, e3. 15 34

# Page 20^page=20
Dual basis of an orthonormal basis Example: The dual basis of an orthonormal basis Let e1 = i1, e2 = i2, e3 = i3 be an orthornormal basis. Then its dual basis is itself an orthonormal basis, consisting of the same vectors: e 1 = e2 × e3 e1 · (e2 × e3) = i2 × i3 i1 · (i2 × i3) = i1 i1 · i1 = i1 1 = i1, and similarly e 2 = i2, e 3 = i3. 16 34

# Page 21^page=21
Summary: Dual Basis Summary: Dual Basis The dual basis ei can be found from the original basis ei via e i = ej × ek ei · (ej × ek) , and the original basis ei can be found from the dual basis ei via ei = ej × ek ei · (ej × ek) , where (i, j, k) is a cyclic permutation of (1, 2, 3). 17 34

# Page 22^page=22
Covariant and contravariant components of a vector

# Page 23^page=23
Vector expansion Vector expansion Let e1 , e2, e3 be any basis of R3. Then, by de˝nition of basis, any vector v = (v1, v2, v3) can be expressed as a linear combination of e1, e2, e3. Example The vector v = (1, 0, 1) can be expressed as v = 1 · i + 0 · j + 1 · k in the basis i = (1, 0, 0), j = (0, 1, 0), k = (0, 0, 1). v = 1 · e1 − 1 · e2 + 1 · e3 in the basis e1 = (1, 0, 0), e2 = (1, 1, 0), e3 = (1, 1, 1). 18 34

# Page 24^page=24
Expanding vectors Expanding vectors Again, given any basis e1, e2, e3, can express any vector A in terms of this basis: A = A1e1 + A2e2 + A3e3, where A1, A2, A3 are scalars (in our context, real numbers). The scalars A1, A2, A3 are known as the expansion coe˚cients . In the following slides, we will learn how to determine the exact values of A1, A2, A3. We will explore the following scenarios: The basis is orthonormal . The basis is orthogonal . The basis is generalised . 19 34

# Page 25^page=25
Vectors in terms of orthonormal bases Vectors in terms of orthonormal bases Let i1 , i2, i3 be an orthonormal basis. Let the expansion of A be given by A = A1i1 + A2i2 + A3i3 = Akik. We can determine the precise value of A1, A2, A3 as follows: since i1 , i2, i3 are orthonormal, we have ik · ij = δkj. Thus, A · ij = (Akik) · ij = A k(ik · ij) = A kδkj = Aj. Consequently, A = (A · i1)i1 + (A · i2)i2 + (A · i3)i3. 20 34

# Page 26^page=26
Vectors in terms of orthogonal bases Vectors in terms of orthogonal bases Previous slide: If i1 , i2, i3 is an orthonormal basis, any vector A can be described by: A = (A · i1)i1 + (A · i2)i2 + (A · i3)i3. Let e1, e2, e3 be an orthogonal basis. Although e1, e2, e3 might not be orthonormal, the following vectors are i1 = e1 e1 , i2 = e2 e2 , i3 = e3 e3 (ei = |ei| for i = 1, 2, 3) Then, by substitution A = A · e1 e2 1 e1 + A · e2 e2 2 e2 + A · e3 e2 3 e3. 21 34

# Page 27^page=27
Vectors in generalised coordinate systems Vectors in generalised coordinate systems To expand a vector in terms of a basis that is not orthogonal, we use the so-called dual basis method . Recall: Dual basis Two bases e1, e2, e3 and e1, e2 , e3 are dual if they satisfy ei · e k = { 0 if i ̸= k, 1 if i = k. In other words, two bases are dual if each vector of one basis is perpendicular to two vectors of the other basis. 22 34

# Page 28^page=28
Expansion coefficients Expansion coe˚cients in generalised coordinate systems Let e1, e2, e3 and e1, e2 , e3 be dual bases. By de˝nition of basis, any vector A can be expanded with respect to each of these bases: 1. Expansion with respect to the basis e1, e2, e3 A = A1e1 + A2e2 + A3e3 = A iei. 2. Expansion with respect to the dual basis e1, e2, e3 A = A1e 1 + A2e 2 + A3e 3 = Aie i. The Ai and Ai are the expansion coe˚cients of A. 23 34

# Page 29^page=29
Contravariant component Contravariant component Let e1, e2, e3 and e1, e2 , e3 be dual bases. By de˝nition of basis, any vector A can be expanded with respect to each of these bases: 1. Expansion with respect to the basis e1, e2, e3 A = A1e1 + A2e2 + A3e3 = A iei. 2. Expansion with respect to the dual basis e1, e2, e3 A = A1e 1 + A2e 2 + A3e 3 = Aie i. The Ai are called the contravariant components of A. 24 34

# Page 30^page=30
Covariant component Covariant component Let e1, e2, e3 and e1, e2 , e3 be dual bases. By de˝nition of basis, any vector A can be expanded with respect to each of these bases: 1. Expansion with respect to the basis e1, e2, e3 A = A1e1 + A2e2 + A3e3 = A iei. 2. Expansion with respect to the dual basis e1, e2, e3 A = A1e 1 + A2e 2 + A3e 3 = Aie i. The Ai are called the covariant components of A . 25 34

# Page 31^page=31
Finding the contravariant and covariant coefficients Finding the contravariant and covariant coe˚cients We will demonstrate: how to compute the contravariant components A1, A2, A3 in terms of the dual basis, and how to compute the covariant components A1, A2, A3 in terms of the original basis. 26 34

# Page 32^page=32
Finding contravariant components Finding contravariant components We want to ˝nd a formula for the contravariant components A1, A2, A3 of a vector A. In other words, we need to ˝nd the coe˚cients A1, A2, A3 in the expansion A = A1e1 + A2e2 + A3e3. Using the identity ek · e i = { 0 if i ̸= k, 1 if i = k = δik. we obtain for each i = 1, 2, 3 A · e i = ( 3∑ k=1 Akek ) · e i = 3∑ k=1 Ak (ek · e i) = 3∑ k=1 Akδik = Ai. 27 34

# Page 33^page=33
Finding covariant components Finding covariant components We want to ˝nd a formula for the covariant components A1, A2, A3 of a vector A. In other words, we need to ˝nd the coe˚cients A1, A2, A3 in the expansion A = A1e 1 + A2e 2 + A3e 3. Using the identity e k · ei = { 0 if i ̸= k, 1 if i = k = δik, we obtain for each i = 1, 2, 3 A · ei = ( 3∑ k=1 Ake k) · ei = 3∑ k=1 Ak (e k · ei) = 3∑ k=1 Akδik = Ai. 28 34

# Page 34^page=34
Summary: Covariant and contravariant components Summary: Covariant and contravariant components Using dual bases, we have found that a vector A can be expanded with respect to the vectors of one basis e1, e2, e3 via A = A1e1 + A2e2 + A3e3 = A iei. with respect to the vectors of the dual basis e1, e2, e3 via A = A1e 1 + A2e 2 + A3e 3 = Aie i, where Ai = A · ei are called the contravariant components of A, and Ai = A · ei are called the covariant components of A. 29 34

Example Example In the previous example, we have found that basis e1 = 2i1 + i3, e2 = i1 + 3i2, e3 = 4i3, has dual basis e 1 =   1/2 −1/6 0   , e 2 =   0 1/3 0   , e 3 =   −1/8 1/24 1/4   . Find the covariant and contravariant components of the vector joining the origin to the point (8, 0, 1). 30 34

# Page 36^page=36
Example - Part 2 Example: Covariant components Finding the covariant components of J = (8, 0, 1)T : The basis is e1 = (2, 0, 1) T , e2 = (1, 3, 0) T , e3 = (0, 0, 4) T . The covariant components J1, J2, J3 are such that J = J1e 1 + J2e 2 + J3e 3 with Ji = J · ei Thus, we have J1 = J · e1 = (8 0 4 ) · (2 0 1 ) = 20, J2 = J · e2 = ( 8 0 4 ) · ( 1 3 0 ) = 8, J3 = J · e3 = (8 0 4 ) · (0 0 4 ) . = 16. 31 34

# Page 37^page=37
Example - Part 3 Example: Contravariant components Finding the contravariant components of J = (8, 0, 4)T : e 1 = (1/2, −1/6, 0) T , e 2 = (0, 1/3, 0) T , e 3 = (−1/8, 1/24, 1/4) T The contravariant components J 1, J 2, J 3 are such that J = J 1e1 + J 2e2 + J 3e3 with J i = J · e i. Thus, we have J 1 = J · e 1 = ( 8 0 4 ) · ( 1 2 − 1 6 0 ) = 4, J 2 = J · e 2 = (8 0 4 ) · (0 1 3 0 ) = 0, J 3 = J · e 3 = ( 8 0 4 ) · (− 1 8 1 24 1 4 ) = 0. 32 34
